## Describe an observational cohort before modeling it

This article assumes the wide-format, identity, mean, and paired-change concepts in [Getting started](frequentist-long-getting-started.html). It adds distributional summaries, variability, association, and stored plots; it does not require longitudinal models. Consider an observational glaucoma-service cohort selected for a history of
elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), measured in mmHg by a consistent hypothetical tonometry
protocol at baseline and three subsequent clinic visits. The objective is
to describe study-eye pressure levels, within-eye changes, and variation.
There is no randomized intervention or concurrent control; a temporal fall
cannot be attributed to treatment from these summaries.

Each person contributes one prespecified study eye: an eligible right eye,
or the left eye when only that eye is eligible, chosen at enrolment. The
participant ID indexes the same eye throughout, and different participants
are the independent sampling units. Entering both eyes as unrelated rows
would require a different dependence model.

The [National Eye Institute](https://www.nei.nih.gov/eye-health-information/eye-conditions-and-diseases/glaucoma/glaucoma-and-eye-pressure)
explains why IOP and glaucoma risk must be interpreted for the individual
eye. Lower pressure is the declared favorable direction for this selected
elevated-pressure teaching cohort, not a universal rule that ever-lower IOP
is desirable or that IOP alone establishes visual benefit.

This is a new glaucoma-monitoring study, separate from the introductory
retinal BCVA dataset. Its assumed decline is chosen to exercise descriptive
methods and is not a recommended target or treatment effect.
The generator assumes a mean underlying pressure of 24 mmHg (between-person
SD 3), a mean fall of 0.9 mmHg per ordered visit (trend SD 0.45), and independent
measurement noise with SD 1.2 mmHg, rounded to 0.1 mmHg. These are simulation
choices, not a validated measurement-error specification. Baseline tonometry
can vary below an individual's prior screening value. Later visits have several
missing measurements. The complete synthetic values are checked to lie between 8 and 40 mmHg as a
plausibility check for this chosen generator, not a definition of a safe or
normal IOP range. The simulation uses visit indices only to construct
data; the analysis treats visits as ordered occasions.

```{r cohort}
library(MIRA)
set.seed(3301)
n <- 64L
usual_iop <- rnorm(n, mean = 24, sd = 3)
individual_trend <- rnorm(n, mean = -0.9, sd = 0.45)
iop_cohort <- data.frame(participant_id = sprintf("G%03d", seq_len(n)))
for (visit in 0:3) {
  iop_cohort[[paste0("iop_visit", visit)]] <- round(usual_iop +
    visit * individual_trend + rnorm(n, sd = 1.2), 1)
}
stopifnot(all(as.matrix(iop_cohort[-1L]) > 8),
          all(as.matrix(iop_cohort[-1L]) < 40))
iop_cohort$iop_visit1[c(8, 31)] <- NA_real_
iop_cohort$iop_visit2[c(7, 19, 44)] <- NA_real_
iop_cohort$iop_visit3[c(7, 19, 40, 55, 62)] <- NA_real_
summary(iop_cohort[-1L])
```

## Request summaries and selected optional components

The configuration requests plots, Pearson/Spearman correlations, and IQR-based
outlier flags while disabling model fitting and arm comparisons. `alpha = 0.05`
gives 95% Student-t intervals. `improvement_direction = "lower"` and
`stable_threshold = 2` supply a declared response convention; two mmHg is an
illustrative threshold, not a validated individual clinical response criterion.

```{r analysis}
description <- mira_info_long(
  iop_cohort, id = "participant_id", outcomes = "IOP",
  time_vars = paste0("iop_visit", 0:3),
  time_labels = c("Baseline", "Month 2", "Month 5", "Month 9"),
  covariates = character(0), alpha = 0.05,
  improvement_direction = "lower", stable_threshold = 2,
  plots = TRUE, correlations = TRUE, outliers = TRUE,
  model = FALSE, arm_tests = FALSE, verbose = FALSE
)
description$overview[c("n_rows", "n_patients", "n_timepoints",
                        "complete_profiles", "complete_profiles_pct")]
description$settings[c("confidence_level", "improvement_direction",
                       "stable_threshold")]
```

Alternatively, `analyses = c("plots", "correlations", "outliers")` selects
exactly those optional modules. A non-`NULL` `analyses` vector replaces all five
individual optional switches. `analyses = "none"` provides the fastest core
workflow, but still includes paired tests and the Friedman branch. Turning off
plots reduces graphics construction; turning off correlations and outlier flags
avoids those calculations. None of these settings changes the observed data.

An explicitly declared outcome prefixes MIRA-owned metrics. Use the documented
metric-name map to select columns without depending on that prefix.

```{r extraction-helper}
metric_columns <- function(table, fields) {
  mapping <- attr(table, "mira_metric_names", exact = TRUE)
  actual <- fields
  matched <- fields %in% names(mapping)
  actual[matched] <- unname(mapping[fields[matched]])
  stopifnot(all(actual %in% names(table)))
  actual
}
show_metrics <- function(table, fields) {
  table[, metric_columns(table, fields), drop = FALSE]
}
```

## Population summaries at each visit

`n` counts finite measurements at that visit. Missing and infinite values have
distinct counts; MIRA treats infinite measurements as unavailable during
analysis. Inspect the availability columns alongside the mean and median.

```{r visit-table}
knitr::kable(
  show_metrics(description$descriptives,
    c("label", "n", "missing", "mean", "sd", "median", "q1", "q3")),
  col.names = c("Visit", "N", "Missing", "Mean", "SD", "Median", "Q1", "Q3"),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Visit-specific availability and IOP distributions (mmHg)."
)
knitr::kable(
  show_metrics(description$descriptives,
    c("label", "mean", "se", "ci_lower", "ci_upper")),
  col.names = c("Visit", "Mean", "SE", "Lower 95% CI", "Upper 95% CI"),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Visit-specific mean IOP and its pointwise uncertainty (mmHg)."
)
iop_values <- as.matrix(iop_cohort[description$time_vars])
stopifnot(identical(description$descriptives$n,
                    as.integer(colSums(is.finite(iop_values)))))
```

The mean and SD describe location and participant-to-participant spread at a
visit. The median and quartiles offer complementary distributional summaries.
The confidence limits estimate uncertainty in a population mean under
independent participant sampling; they are neither prediction intervals nor
within-person change intervals. All intervals here are pointwise, rather than
a simultaneous band over visits. A confidence interval's nominal level does
not mean that the fixed population mean has a 95% frequentist probability of
lying inside this particular calculated interval.

The changing denominator matters. If people with high pressures preferentially
miss later visits, an available-case mean can fall even without comparable
individual improvement. The artificial missingness here is assigned to fixed
indices, but a real study needs a substantive missing-data investigation.

## Paired changes and individual trajectories

For each ordered pair of visits, MIRA calculates changes using only people
observed at both visits. We select all baseline-to-follow-up rows by name.

```{r changes}
from_baseline <- description$change[
  description$change$from == "iop_visit0", , drop = FALSE]
knitr::kable(
  show_metrics(from_baseline,
    c("to_label", "n", "mean_change", "sd_change", "ci_lower", "ci_upper",
      "cohens_dz")),
  col.names = c("Visit", "N", "Mean change", "SD change", "Lower 95% CI",
                "Upper 95% CI", "Cohen's dz"),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Paired follow-up-minus-baseline IOP changes (mmHg)."
)
complete_final <- complete.cases(iop_cohort[c("iop_visit0", "iop_visit3")])
final_differences <- iop_cohort$iop_visit3[complete_final] -
  iop_cohort$iop_visit0[complete_final]
computed_change <- mean(final_differences)
final_row <- from_baseline[from_baseline$to == "iop_visit3", , drop = FALSE]
half_width <- qt(0.975, df = length(final_differences) - 1L) *
  sd(final_differences) / sqrt(length(final_differences))
stopifnot(nrow(final_row) == 1L, final_row$n == sum(complete_final),
  isTRUE(all.equal(final_row[[metric_columns(final_row, "mean_change")]],
                   computed_change)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(unname(unlist(show_metrics(final_row,
    c("ci_lower", "ci_upper")))),
    computed_change + c(-1, 1) * half_width)))
```

Negative change indicates lower IOP in mmHg; the favorable label follows
the explicitly chosen elevated-pressure cohort interpretation. The SD of change describes heterogeneity
in paired differences. Cohen's `dz` divides the mean paired difference by its
SD; it is not the independent-groups standardized mean difference. Its value
depends on within-person variability and correlation, so it should accompany
the effect in original units rather than replace it.

Individual trajectories distinguish an average decline from a uniform response.
The relative change uses `100 * (final - baseline) / abs(baseline)` for a
nonzero finite baseline. That percentage is meaningful only on an appropriate
measurement scale and can be unstable near zero.

```{r trajectories}
head(show_metrics(description$trajectories,
  c("patient", "baseline", "final", "absolute_change",
    "relative_change_percent", "direction", "clinical_direction")))
table(description$trajectories$clinical_direction, useNA = "ifany")
```

Response labels compare the measured change with the supplied threshold; they
do not account for individual measurement error or establish a treatment
effect. A missing baseline or final measurement leaves that trajectory change
unavailable even when intermediate observations exist.

## Correlation and variability answer different questions

Pearson correlation summarizes linear association between visit measurements;
Spearman correlation summarizes association between ranks. Neither measures
agreement with the identity line, and a high correlation can coexist with a
systematic shift in mean pressure. Pairwise-complete samples can differ across
matrix cells; always inspect `pairwise_n`.

```{r correlations}
round(description$correlations$pearson, 2)
round(description$correlations$spearman, 2)
description$correlations$pairwise_n
stopifnot(description$correlations$pairwise_n["iop_visit0", "iop_visit3"] ==
            sum(complete_final))
```

To isolate why association is different from agreement, keep the same baseline
IOP values and construct an artificial second measurement exactly 2 mmHg
higher for every person. Predict the Pearson correlation and mean change
before reading the solution. This arithmetic demonstration is separate from
the observed follow-up data above and does not alter `description`.

```{r correlation-shift-checkpoint}
shifted_iop <- iop_cohort$iop_visit0 + 2
shift_correlation <- cor(iop_cohort$iop_visit0, shifted_iop)
shift_mean_change <- mean(shifted_iop - iop_cohort$iop_visit0)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Pearson_correlation = shift_correlation,
  Mean_change_mmHg = shift_mean_change
), digits = 2,
caption = "Solution: perfect association coexists with a systematic 2-mmHg increase.")
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(shift_correlation, 1)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(shift_mean_change, 2)))
```

Adding a constant preserves the ordering and linear association of people,
so the correlation is one, yet every person changes by 2 mmHg. Correlation
alone cannot establish stability, agreement, or absence of systematic change.

The within-participant SD is the ordinary sample SD of all finite residuals
after subtracting each participant's available-visit mean. Its denominator is
the number of finite measurements minus one; it is not the pooled ANOVA
within-participant SD, which would subtract the number of participant means
estimated. This descriptive residual spread combines measurement noise and
temporal variation. The between-participant SD is the ordinary sample SD of
available-visit participant means, giving each available participant mean equal
weight even when observation counts differ. Neither is automatically a variance
component from a longitudinal model.

```{r variability}
knitr::kable(
  show_metrics(description$variability,
    c("between_subject_sd", "within_subject_sd",
      "ICC_anova_complete_profiles", "ICC_model", "ICC")),
  col.names = c("Between-person SD", "Within-person SD", "ICC(1,1)",
                "Model ICC", "Preferred ICC"),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Participant variability and available intraclass-correlation estimates."
)
```

Here the ICC concerns repeated IOP observations of the selected eye across
visits; it is not an inter-eye correlation or agreement estimate for fellow eyes.

With models disabled, `ICC_model` is unavailable and the preferred `ICC` uses
the complete-profile one-way ICC(1,1). For `k` visits, that estimate is
`(MS_between - MS_within) / (MS_between + (k - 1) * MS_within)`.
It uses a different sample from a pairwise correlation. A time trend enters the
within-participant variation, so this ICC should not be interpreted as a pure
test-retest reliability coefficient without assumptions about stability and
exchangeability. Negative ANOVA ICC estimates are possible. When a fitted
random-intercept model is available, the preferred ICC instead uses its
random-intercept variance divided by random-intercept plus residual variance;
always identify the estimator being reported.

The following check reconstructs the balanced one-way ANOVA independently
from complete profiles. Its sample can be smaller than either the number with
any measurement or the number contributing to a particular paired change.
The residual-SD check uses all available measurements instead.

```{r verify-variability}
complete_profiles <- apply(is.finite(iop_values), 1L, all)
balanced <- iop_values[complete_profiles, , drop = FALSE]
k <- ncol(balanced)
icc_data <- data.frame(
  value = as.vector(t(balanced)),
  participant = factor(rep(seq_len(nrow(balanced)), each = k))
)
one_way <- anova(lm(value ~ participant, data = icc_data))
ms_between <- one_way$`Mean Sq`[[1L]]
ms_within <- one_way$`Mean Sq`[[2L]]
icc_check <- (ms_between - ms_within) /
  (ms_between + (k - 1L) * ms_within)
residuals <- iop_values - rowMeans(iop_values, na.rm = TRUE)
stopifnot(description$overview$complete_profiles == nrow(balanced),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    description$variability[[metric_columns(description$variability,
      "ICC_anova_complete_profiles")]], icc_check)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    description$variability[[metric_columns(description$variability,
      "within_subject_sd")]], sd(residuals[is.finite(residuals)]))))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Summary = c("Any observed visit", "Baseline and final", "All four visits"),
  Participants = c(sum(rowSums(is.finite(iop_values)) > 0L),
                   sum(complete_final), sum(complete_profiles))
), caption = "Participants and their single study eyes contributing to different IOP summaries.")
```

## Inspect plots and flagged observations

MIRA stores named `ggplot` objects, permitting ordinary printing and further
customization. The first figure joins observations from the same participant;
the second shows visit-specific means and their confidence limits. Time labels
are equally spaced categories: physical intervals of 2, 3, and 4 months are
not displayed proportionally.

```{r plot-inventory}
names(description$plots)
stopifnot(inherits(description$plots$spaghetti, "ggplot"),
          inherits(description$plots$mean_ci, "ggplot"))
```

```{r trajectories-figure, fig.cap="Synthetic IOP (mmHg) in 64 prespecified study eyes from 64 participants over four ordered visits. Available observations are connected across gaps; lines do not impute missing visits. The black line and band show available-case means and pointwise 95% mean confidence intervals. Visits are equally spaced on the axis despite unequal elapsed times."}
print(description$plots$spaghetti + ggplot2::labs(y = "IOP (mmHg)"))
```

```{r means-figure, fig.cap="Available-case study-eye IOP means (mmHg) with pointwise 95% confidence intervals. Visit samples are 64, 62, 61, and 59 participants; changing participants can affect the pattern. Confidence intervals describe mean uncertainty, not individual variation. The horizontal axis shows ordered visits."}
print(description$plots$mean_ci + ggplot2::labs(y = "IOP (mmHg)"))
```

The `boxplot` and `correlation_heatmap` objects provide distributional and
association views. `outliers$by_time` and `outliers$change` contain IQR-rule
diagnostics. These flags request investigation of data validity and scientific
context; MIRA does not delete flagged observations automatically.

```{r outliers}
description$outliers$note
data.frame(
  visit = names(description$outliers$by_time),
  flagged_n = vapply(description$outliers$by_time, nrow, integer(1L))
)
data.frame(
  comparison = names(description$outliers$change),
  flagged_n = vapply(description$outliers$change, nrow, integer(1L))
)
head(description$outliers$by_time[["iop_visit0"]])
```

## Keep descriptive and inferential conclusions distinct

Although the object contains descriptive summaries, the paired t tests,
asymptotic signed-rank tests, and complete-profile Friedman test also perform
inference. The paired t test concerns a mean difference and requires
appropriate sampling and a defensible approximation for the difference
distribution. Signed-rank interpretation involves the distribution and
symmetry of paired differences; it is not an assumption-free test of means.
The Friedman branch compares repeated ranks on complete profiles, with
participants as blocks.

```{r core-inference-status}
description$advanced_tests$friedman[c("performed", "reason_skipped")]
inference_display <- show_metrics(description$change,
  c("from_label", "to_label", "n", "paired_t_p", "paired_t_p_adj"))
for (column in metric_columns(description$change,
  c("paired_t_p", "paired_t_p_adj"))) {
  inference_display[[column]] <- format.pval(inference_display[[column]],
                                            digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
}
knitr::kable(inference_display,
  col.names = c("From", "To", "N", "Paired t p", "Holm p"),
  caption = "Pairwise-complete mean-change tests; display formatting does not alter the analysis.")
```

The default Holm adjustment applies separately to the finite paired-t and
signed-rank p-values across the selected visit-pair comparisons. It does not
turn descriptive confidence limits into simultaneous intervals or cover every
analysis in the object. Prespecify a scientific hypothesis family before
interpreting multiple tests; effect magnitude, uncertainty, missingness, and
clinical relevance remain central. Continue with
[treatment-group comparisons](frequentist-long-treatment-groups.html) and
[missing-data analysis](frequentist-long-missing-data.html) before drawing
study-level conclusions.
